items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: my first group that I performed with in New York City was with Jackie McLean. He trained Bobby Hutcherson, Charles Tolliver, and let me see, and myself.

ctx.x: Well my question is, moving from placing quarter notes and swing and playing on top of the beat, this was a totally different task for you it seems like, playing a bass line repetitively in some cases basically the similar thing all the way through, while other players did their explorations. Like you were the anchor. And I wonder if you enjoyed that role, for sometimes the songs could go on for eight or nine minutes. How do you keep your concentration?

You don’t concentrate, you just feel it. Something like that, by that I mean it’s just a vibe. You are now as a bassist, you are now being rather responsible to maintain the bass line that would support all that is happening beyond you melodically, harmonically, etcetera, etcetera. It was something, quite frankly, that I was already sort of familiar with. Number one my second group — my first group that I performed with in New York City was with Jackie McLean. He trained Bobby Hutcherson, Charles Tolliver, and…
This is sort of a personal question, do you feel you are a spiritual man? Does faith play a significant role in your life?

items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: Jackie McLean, we did that when things were more or less in line structurally, etcetera, etcetera.

ctx.x: Jackie McLean, we did that when things were more or less in line structurally, etcetera, etcetera. You know you would open up. That’s when they had those tapes, you know those big thick tapes. But with Pharoah I don’t recall ever doing that with anything, the things were like from A all the way to Z and past, with fury, either be it in the quietest of the night or the loudest of the center of the city.
Did you ever read reviews on some of these recordings or live gigs with Pharoah where the reviewer called the music “angry?”
